relations.note: Brétigny (1360) truce: England renounces the French crown for full sovereignty over an enlarged Aquitaine
Gallipoli (1354) becomes a permanent Ottoman bridgehead into Europe
Algirdas presses into the Horde's weakening grip on the Dnieper basin
War of the Two Pedros begins over rival succession claims
The 'Great Troubles' loosen the Horde's grip on Rus tribute collection
Renewed maritime rivalry despite both republics' plague losses

slices.label: Kulikovo, the Krewo union, and Ottoman vassals in the Balkans
events: Dmitri Donskoi defeats Mamai's Golden Horde army at Kulikovo, a symbolic first crack in the Tatar yoke
After Maritsa (1371) the Ottomans reduce Macedonia and Bulgaria to tribute-paying vassals; Serbia's Lazar still independent
The Great Schism (1378) splits the Latin Church between rival popes at Rome and Avignon
slices.connectivityNote: Slow recovery from plague: Hanseatic and Venetian trade rebuilding, but Ottoman advances and the Western Schism add new friction.

entities.name: Kingdom of England
entities.note: Peasants' Revolt (1381, imminent) brews under Richard II's minority; Aquitaine slowly bleeding back to France.

entities.name: Kingdom of Castile
entities.note: Trastámara dynasty secure since 1369; close ally of France against England.

entities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
entities.note: Succession crisis brewing toward the 1383-85 interregnum.

entities.name: Marinid Sultanate
entities.note: Dynasty weakening, real power shifting to Wattasid viziers.

entities.name: Kingdom of France
entities.note: Charles V's reconquests have clawed back much of Brétigny's territory before his death (1380).

entities.name: Holy Roman Empire
entities.note: Wenceslas IV's ineffective rule; princely and city leagues jostle for power.

entities.name: Swiss Confederacy
entities.note: Sempach (1386, imminent) will confirm Confederate independence from Habsburg Austria.

entities.name: County of Flanders
entities.note: Urban revolts (Ghent under Philip van Artevelde) against the count and French crown.

entities.name: Republic of Genoa
entities.note: War of Chioggia against Venice (1378-81) nearly ruinous for both republics.

entities.name: Papal States
entities.note: Western Schism (1378): rival popes at Rome and Avignon split Latin Christendom.

entities.name: Angevin Kingdom of Naples
entities.note: Joanna I's succession crisis feeds directly into the Great Schism's politics.

entities.name: Kingdom of Denmark
entities.note: Olaf II, son of Valdemar IV and Margaret, unites Denmark and Norway's crowns (1380).

entities.name: Kingdom of Norway
entities.note: Enters personal union with Denmark under young Olaf II (1380).

entities.name: Kingdom of Sweden
entities.note: Albert of Mecklenburg's unpopular reign; Margaret of Denmark-Norway waiting in the wings.

entities.name: Teutonic Order
entities.note: Continues crusading raids into pagan Lithuania even as Jogaila's conversion looms.

entities.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
entities.note: Algirdas's Rus conquests (Kyiv 1362, Blue Waters victory) peak; Jogaila's succession and the Krewo union with Poland are imminent (1385-86).

entities.name: Kingdom of Poland
entities.note: Louis of Hungary's daughter Jadwiga will inherit the crown (1384), setting up the Krewo union with Lithuania.

entities.name: Grand Duchy of Muscovy
entities.note: Dmitri Donskoi defeats Mamai at Kulikovo (Sept 1380) - a symbolic victory, though the Horde's power is not yet broken.

entities.name: Golden Horde
entities.note: Mamai's defeat at Kulikovo caps the 'Great Troubles'; Tokhtamysh will soon reunite the Horde and sack Moscow (1382).

entities.name: Kingdom of Hungary
entities.note: Louis the Great dies (1382, imminent), leaving only daughters and a succession crisis.

entities.name: Banate of Bosnia
entities.note: Tvrtko I building toward his 1377 royal coronation's full authority.

entities.name: Republic of Venice
entities.note: War of Chioggia against Genoa (1378-81) brings the republic to the brink before a hard-won victory.

entities.name: Kingdom of Serbia
entities.note: Prince Lazar rules a reduced Serbian heartland after Dušan's empire fragmented; still independent, Kosovo (1389) still ahead.

entities.name: Despotate of Epirus
entities.note: Reformed under Serbian-descended despots at Ioannina; Albanian lords (Balša, Thopia, Kastrioti) hold the coast.

entities.name: Second Bulgarian Empire
entities.note: Ivan Shishman's Tarnovo tsardom now an Ottoman tributary after Maritsa (1371).

entities.name: Byzantine Empire
entities.note: John V, himself an Ottoman vassal since 1373, holds little beyond Constantinople's walls.

entities.name: Ottoman Beylik/Sultanate
entities.note: Murad I annexes Thrace and vassalizes Macedonia's lords after crushing the Serbian nobility at Maritsa (1371).

entities.name: Duchy of Athens
entities.note: Passing from Catalan to Florentine (Acciaiuoli) control by 1388.

entities.name: Principality of Achaea
entities.note: The Navarrese Company seizes the principality (1381).

entities.name: Anatolian Turkish Beyliks
entities.note: Increasingly squeezed and absorbed by Ottoman expansion.

entities.name: Karamanid Beylik
entities.note: Chief rival to Ottoman power in Anatolia.

entities.name: Jalayirid Sultanate
entities.note: Sultan Ahmad Jalayir's realm now faces a new threat: Timur's rising power in Central Asia.

entities.name: Kingdom of Cilician Armenia
entities.note: Final Mamluk conquest (1375) has already extinguished the kingdom; Lusignan claimants hold only the title.

entities.name: Lusignan Kingdom of Cyprus
entities.note: Genoese seize Famagusta (1373-74), crippling Cypriot trade revenue.

entities.name: Mamluk Sultanate
entities.note: Barquq founds the Circassian Burji dynasty (1382), ending Turkic Bahri Mamluk rule.

relations.note: Kulikovo (1380): Dmitri Donskoi's symbolic victory over Mamai
Maritsa (1371) breaks the Serbian nobility, opening Macedonia and Bulgaria to vassalage
War of Chioggia (1378-81), the two republics' most brutal conflict
Krewo union (1385-86) approaching: Jogaila to marry Jadwiga and christianize Lithuania
Western Schism politics entangle Neapolitan succession claims
Lithuania's Rus conquests carve deep into former Horde tributary lands

slices.label: Nicopolis: the last great crusade fails
events: Bayezid I annihilates a pan-European crusader army at Nicopolis on the Danube
Bulgaria's Tarnovo tsardom (fallen 1393) and Vidin (fallen 1396) are fully annexed; the Second Bulgarian Empire ends
Constantinople endures a fourth year of Ottoman blockade; Timur's armies gut the Golden Horde and Jalayirid Mesopotamia alike
slices.connectivityNote: Hanseatic and Venetian trade recovering steadily, but Ottoman consolidation in the Balkans and Timur's rampage in the east add fresh disruption.

entities.name: Kingdom of England
entities.note: Richard II's uneasy later reign; Aquitaine reduced but still substantial after Charles V's reconquests.

entities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
entities.note: Aviz dynasty secure since the 1385 Battle of Aljubarrota confirmed independence from Castile.

entities.name: Kingdom of France
entities.note: Charles VI's bouts of madness (from 1392) let royal uncles and Burgundy dominate the government.

entities.name: Valois Burgundy
entities.note: Philip the Bold unites Burgundy and Flanders (1384) into Europe's rising power; his son led the doomed Nicopolis crusade.

entities.name: Holy Roman Empire
entities.note: Wenceslas IV's weak rule; town leagues and princely feuds proliferate.

entities.name: Swiss Confederacy
entities.note: Confederate victory at Sempach (1386) confirms independence from Habsburg Austria.

entities.name: Kingdom of Bohemia
entities.note: Wenceslas IV (also nominal HRE king) faces baronial revolt at home.

entities.name: Republic of Genoa
entities.note: Submits to French royal protection (1396) to escape internal factional chaos.

entities.name: Papal States
entities.note: Western Schism unresolved; Boniface IX at Rome, Benedict XIII at Avignon.

entities.name: Duchy of Milan
entities.note: Gian Galeazzo Visconti, newly titled duke (1395), the most feared power-broker in Italy.

entities.name: Angevin Kingdom of Naples
entities.note: Ladislaus of Durazzo consolidating after decades of Angevin succession wars.

entities.name: Republic of Pisa
entities.note: Falling into Florentine and Milanese orbits; sold to Milan in 1399.

entities.name: Kingdom of Denmark
entities.note: Margaret I rules Denmark, Norway and (since Falköping, 1389) Sweden; the formal Kalmar Union follows in 1397.

entities.name: Kingdom of Norway
entities.note: In personal union with Denmark under Margaret I since 1380.

entities.name: Kingdom of Sweden
entities.note: Under Margaret I's rule since 1389; formal Kalmar Union with Denmark and Norway one year away.

entities.name: Teutonic Order
entities.note: Losing its crusading rationale now that Lithuania has converted to Christianity (1386).

entities.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
entities.note: Vytautas rules under Jogaila's Polish crown; Europe's largest state by area, spanning Belarus, Kyiv and Volhynia.

entities.name: Kingdom of Poland
entities.note: Jogaila (Władysław II Jagiełło) rules jointly with Lithuania since the Union of Krewo (1385-86) and his baptism.

entities.name: Grand Duchy of Muscovy
entities.note: Vasily I navigates continued Tatar overlordship after Tokhtamysh's sack of Moscow (1382).

entities.name: Golden Horde
entities.note: Timur crushes Tokhtamysh's armies (1391, 1395) and sacks Sarai, shattering the Horde's power for a generation.

entities.name: Voivodeship of Wallachia
entities.note: Mircea the Elder fights at Nicopolis and faces growing Ottoman pressure for tribute.

entities.name: Kingdom of Hungary
entities.note: Sigismund of Luxembourg leads the crusader army to catastrophic defeat at Nicopolis (1396), barely escaping by boat.

entities.name: Banate of Bosnia
entities.note: Kingdom fragmenting among rival nobles since Tvrtko I's death (1391).

entities.name: Republic of Venice
entities.note: Neutral profiteer of the Nicopolis disaster, ferrying survivors home for a fee.

entities.name: Kingdom of Serbia
entities.note: Stefan Lazarević rules as an Ottoman vassal, his knights fighting FOR Bayezid at Nicopolis.

entities.name: Despotate of Epirus
entities.note: Esau Buondelmonti's small despotate at Ioannina, hemmed in by Ottoman pressure from the east.

entities.name: Byzantine Empire
entities.note: Constantinople in its fourth year of Ottoman blockade (since 1394); Manuel II will soon tour Western courts begging for aid.

entities.name: Ottoman Beylik/Sultanate
entities.note: Bayezid annihilates the Nicopolis crusade, annexes Bulgaria outright (Tarnovo 1393, Vidin 1396), vassalizes Macedonia, Albania and Serbia.

entities.name: Duchy of Athens
entities.note: Under Florentine Acciaiuoli rule since 1388.

entities.name: Principality of Achaea
entities.note: The Navarrese Company's rule is fragile and shrinking under Byzantine and Ottoman pressure.

entities.name: Karamanid Beylik
entities.note: Chief remaining rival to Ottoman power in Anatolia, Bayezid campaigning against it this very year.

entities.name: Timurid Empire
entities.note: Timur sacks Baghdad (1393) and ravages Georgia, absorbing former Jalayirid lands ahead of his clash with Bayezid (1402).

entities.name: Empire of Trebizond
entities.note: Pays tribute to both Timur and the Ottomans to survive.

entities.name: Mamluk Sultanate
entities.note: Barquq's Circassian Mamluks watch Timur's rise in Mesopotamia with alarm.

entities.name: Kingdom of Georgia
entities.note: Timur's repeated invasions (from 1386) devastate the kingdom.

Constantinople under close blockade since 1394

famousBorders.name: Portugal-Spain (Treaty of Alcanices)
famousBorders.note: Europe's oldest near-unchanged border (1,234 km), set 1297. Sole dispute: Olivenza, held by Spain since 1801.

famousBorders.name: Anglo-Scottish border (Treaty of York)
famousBorders.note: Fixed 1237; only Berwick (1482) and the Debatable Lands (1552) moved since. Internal UK line after 1707.

famousBorders.name: France-Spain (Treaty of the Pyrenees)
famousBorders.note: Crest-line border of 1659, demarcated by the Bayonne treaties 1856-68; leaves Llivia as a Spanish exclave.

famousBorders.name: Norway-Russia (Treaty of Novgorod)
famousBorders.note: 1326 peace set Arctic tribute zones; the exact line was drawn 1826. Today NATO's oldest quiet frontier with Russia.

famousBorders.name: Andorra (Pareage of 1278)
famousBorders.note: Feudal charter split sovereignty between Foix and Urgell; the valleys' borders have not moved since.

famousBorders.name: San Marino
famousBorders.note: Republic by legend since 301 CE; borders unchanged since the 1463 enlargement - the world's oldest state line.

famousBorders.name: Swiss frontiers (Congress of Vienna)
famousBorders.note: Borders and perpetual neutrality fixed 1815; untouched by two world wars.

famousBorders.name: Rhine-Danube Roman limes
famousBorders.note: Rome's river frontier for four centuries; its ghost lingers in later borders, dialects and the wine-beer line.

famousBorders.name: Eider line (Denmark-Empire)
famousBorders.note: The Treaty of Heiligen made the Eider Denmark's southern edge for a millennium, until the 1864 war.

famousBorders.name: Offa's Dyke (England-Wales)
famousBorders.note: Mercian earthwork of c. 785 still shadows the modern English-Welsh boundary.

famousBorders.name: Ottoman-Habsburg Military Frontier
famousBorders.note: Fortified soldier-settler cordon (Militaergrenze) guarding the Habsburg south against the Ottomans for 350 years.

famousBorders.name: Oder-Neisse line (Germany-Poland)
famousBorders.note: Drawn at Potsdam 1945; Germany renounced the lands beyond it, with final recognition in the 1990 treaty.

famousBorders.name: Curzon line (Poland's eastern border)
famousBorders.note: Proposed 1919, imposed at Yalta/Potsdam 1945; now the EU-Schengen edge facing Belarus and Ukraine.

famousBorders.name: Green Line, Cyprus
famousBorders.note: UN buffer zone along the August 1974 ceasefire; 180 km slicing the island - and Nicosia - in two.

tradeSystems.name: Bronze Age tin, copper & amber routes
tradeSystems.note: Palace-to-palace circuits: Cypriot copper, eastern tin, Baltic amber; the Uluburun wreck carried goods of seven cultures.

tradeSystems.name: Phoenician maritime network
tradeSystems.note: Tyre and Sidon strung colonies from Cyprus to Gadir; Tartessian silver flowed east past Carthage.

tradeSystems.name: Greek colonial network
tradeSystems.note: Hundreds of poleis from Massalia to Crimea traded grain, wine, oil and ideas across a Greek-speaking sea.

tradeSystems.name: Persian Royal Road
tradeSystems.note: 2,700 km of posting stations from Sardis toward Susa; royal couriers in a week, caravans in three months.

tradeSystems.name: Hellenistic grain & luxury circuit
tradeSystems.note: Alexandria, Rhodes and Delos hubbed a koine-Greek market binding Egypt, Syria and the Aegean.

tradeSystems.name: Roman Mare Nostrum
tradeSystems.note: Grain fleets, 80,000 km of roads and a pirate-free sea: the ancient world's connectivity peak under the Pax Romana.

tradeSystems.name: Radhanite network
tradeSystems.note: Jewish merchants bridged Christendom and Islam from the Rhone to Cathay - furs and swords east, silk and spice west.

tradeSystems.name: Varangian river routes
tradeSystems.note: Norse-Rus portages linked the Baltic to Byzantium and the Caliphate; Arab dirhams piled up in Swedish hoards.

tradeSystems.name: Venice & Genoa galley empires
tradeSystems.note: Rival sea empires: Venice ruled the Levant runs, Genoa the Black Sea; both opened sea lanes to Flanders after 1277.

tradeSystems.name: Champagne fairs
tradeSystems.note: A six-fair annual cycle where Flemish cloth met Italian silver and Levant spices - medieval Europe's clearing house.

tradeSystems.name: Hanseatic League
tradeSystems.note: Luebeck-led league of ~200 towns; kontors at Novgorod, Bergen, Bruges and London moved fur, fish, wax and grain.

tradeSystems.name: Pax Mongolica Silk Road
tradeSystems.note: 'The road to Cathay is perfectly safe, day or night' - Pegolotti. Caffa and Tana funneled Asia into Genoese holds.

tradeSystems.name: Dutch entrepot & Baltic 'mother trade'
tradeSystems.note: Fluyts hauled Danzig grain and Norway timber to Amsterdam, redistributing south for salt, wine and silver.

tradeSystems.name: Levant companies (English & French)
tradeSystems.note: Marseille and London ran cloth-for-silk exchanges with Smyrna, Aleppo and Alexandria under Ottoman capitulations.

tradeSystems.name: Atlantic age of sail (London hub)
tradeSystems.note: London eclipsed Amsterdam; colonial sugar and cotton met Baltic stores and Iberian wine - ocean legs leave the map.

tradeSystems.name: Steam, rail & Suez (first globalization)
tradeSystems.note: Steamships through Suez (1869), railways and telegraphs drove trade to ~30% of world GDP by 1913.

tradeSystems.name: COMECON bloc trade
tradeSystems.note: Commerce re-routed behind the Iron Curtain: Moscow-centered barter of oil, machinery and grain among socialist states.

tradeSystems.name: EU single market & Schengen
tradeSystems.note: Free movement of goods, people, capital and services since 1993; passport-free Schengen from 1995 - history's peak.

benchmarks.note: First farming-based population growth; Egypt's Nile floodplain already supports the map's densest cluster.
Old Kingdom Egypt's pyramid-building state is the map's first true demographic and fiscal concentration; Europe still thinly settled.
Middle Kingdom Egypt recovers from the First Intermediate Period; Minoan Crete's first palaces mark the Aegean's takeoff.
Palatial Bronze Age growth: Egypt, the Hittites and the Minoans all expand on irrigated or palace-redistributed surplus.
Late Bronze Age population peak just before the palatial world's systemic collapse.
Post-collapse recovery still incomplete in the east (Aegean/Anatolia lost most of their Bronze Age peak c.1100-1000 BCE); Iron Age farming pushes numbers up in temperate Europe regardless.
Classical urbanization: Persian satrapal wealth, Greek poleis and an expanding Carthage all growing on trade and grain surplus.
Hellenistic and Punic Mediterranean at its commercial height, just before Rome's conquests absorb it wholesale.
Augustan peace unifies almost the entire map under one administration; monetized, tax-fed growth follows.
Roman demographic plateau near its ancient peak, but the Antonine Plague (165-180) has already cut the growth rate.
Crisis-of-the-3rd-century plagues, civil wars and Germanic migrations reverse two centuries of Roman growth.
Justinianic Plague (from 541) and endless Byzantine-Sassanid war produce antiquity's deepest population trough.
Carolingian agricultural revival in the west; Abbasid-era prosperity lifts Egypt and the Levant.
The medieval climate optimum begins a long, nearly unbroken expansion across the whole map.
High medieval takeoff: three-field rotation, forest clearance and the commercial revolution drive Europe past 55 million.
Medieval population ceiling reached just before catastrophe; Europe, Egypt and the Levant are all near their pre-modern peaks.
The Black Death (1347-51) and its recurring waves cut roughly a third off the map's population within two generations.
Renaissance-era recovery is essentially complete north of the Alps; Ottoman conquests reorganize the eastern rim.
Ottoman and Habsburg territorial peaks coincide with steady population growth, though not yet back above the pre-Black-Death growth rate.
Growth slows overall: the Ottoman core stagnates and France plateaus, while Russia and England begin accelerating.
Pre-industrial demographic take-off begins in Britain and Russia; most of the map is still Malthusian.
The agricultural and early industrial revolution breaks the old Malthusian ceiling in northwest Europe first.
Industrializing Europe adds nearly 80 million in a single generation; Egypt's Muhammad Ali-era cotton boom also drives fast growth.
Second Industrial Revolution and public-health gains drive the fastest sustained growth the map has ever recorded.
Peak of the first globalization era; mass emigration to the Americas is the only real brake on European growth.
WWI (~17M dead) and the 1918-20 flu slow growth sharply; the USSR's collectivization famines are just ahead.
Postwar count: WWII killed roughly 40 million Europeans including the Holocaust, a loss the following baby boom already masks here.
Postwar baby boom plus the Green Revolution in Egypt/Maghreb/Anatolia drive the fastest map-wide growth on record.
European growth has nearly stopped (below-replacement fertility almost everywhere) while Egypt, the Maghreb and Anatolia keep booming.
Europe's population has plateaued or begun to shrink; almost all further map growth now comes from Egypt, the Maghreb and Anatolia.
